item.title: Homeland Security Agents Search Home of Rep. Ilhan Omar
item.description:
Federal agents executed a search warrant at the home of Representative Ilhan Omar of Minnesota on Monday, according to three people briefed on the matter, the kind of investigative step the Justice Department has long shied away from so close to an election.

The court-approved search of her Washington-area home comes after Department of Homeland Security officials said in recent months that they were investigating Ms. Omar, a Democrat, over her family’s immigration paperwork. More recently, some federal investigators have also sought to investigate other issues, such as Ms. Omar’s finances, campaign funds and interactions with a foreign citizen, as The New York Times previously reported.

The three people who described the execution of the search warrant spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss it.

The search warrant, executed 22 days before Election Day, lists a series of potential immigration crimes under investigation, including false statements and fraud in immigration paperwork, as well as a general conspiracy charge, according to a person familiar with the document.

A Justice Department spokeswoman said that Homeland Security Investigations agents — a part of Immigration and Customs Enforcement — executed a judicially authorized search of a home in the Washington area, as part of an “ongoing federal criminal investigation.” The spokeswoman declined to comment further.

What you should know about anonymous sources. The Times makes a careful decision any time it shields the identity of a source. The information the source supplies must be newsworthy, credible and give readers genuine insight.

Jackie Rogers, Ms. Omar’s spokeswoman, did not immediately respond to requests for comment sent by email and text message Monday morning.

In September, Markwayne Mullin, the Homeland Security secretary, said his department was investigating issues surrounding Ms. Omar and her family’s immigration to the United States, and suggested the end result could be deportation.

Ms. Omar was born in Mogadishu, Somalia, in the early 1980s. Her family fled their hometown when she was around 8, as a civil war engulfed the country, according to a memoir she wrote. In the mid-1990s, after spending time at a refugee camp in Kenya, Ms. Omar and her relatives were admitted as refugees in the United States. They started a new life in Minnesota, which is home to the largest Somali diaspora in the United States.

Ms. Omar has long said that suggestions that she and her family committed immigration fraud were false and politically motivated.

“I will say it again so it’s as clear as possible: I’m not at all worried about these investigations, because they are complete shams,” she wrote in a fund-raising email in September.

Monday’s search of her home, which was reported earlier by Fox News, takes place within the 60-day window before an election. Justice Department policy has long urged prosecutors not to take any overt, unnecessary investigative steps that could affect an election during that period — especially if such actions could be taken after the election without causing any harm to the investigation. The guiding principle of the 60-day rule is that prosecutors should exercise caution in regard to politically sensitive cases.

The rule is not absolute, and there are exceptions, such as instances where prosecutors believe evidence could be destroyed, ongoing crimes are being committed, or people are in danger. The rule is also largely an interpretation of Justice Department regulations, and as such has been the subject of significant debate about its exact parameters. For many years, however, Justice Department officials have concluded that a publicly observable search — such as of a politician’s home or business — is the kind of overt activity that should be avoided during the 60-day period.

In the last federal election, Mr. Trump cited the 60-day rule in his own criminal cases to accuse the department of acting improperly in 2024 as he campaigned for election. He and his lawyers, some of whom now run the Justice Department, argued that the special counsel, Jack Smith, broke the 60-day rule when he filed court papers in September 2024 describing the evidence supporting charges that Mr. Trump conspired to obstruct the results of the 2020 election. In that instance, however, the key decisions were made by the courts, which are not subject to the department policy.

Ms. Omar has represented a solidly blue district that includes Minneapolis since 2019, and she faced no serious competitors during the primary this year.

item.title: Actress Selma Blair Is Arrested in Assault on Flight Attendants
item.description:
The actress Selma Blair was arrested late on Sunday after the police responded to a call about a “physically abusive passenger” aboard a flight that had landed at Kennedy Airport in New York, the Port Authority Police Department said.

The police said two flight attendants reported injuries on a Delta Air Lines flight from Los Angeles to New York.

One flight attendant was taken to a hospital for further evaluation. Details about the attendants’ injuries were not immediately available.

Ms. Blair, 54, was taken into custody just after 11 p.m. and was then taken to a hospital, the Port Authority Police Department said.

The F.B.I., which is responsible for investigating assaults on airplanes, said on Monday that it was investigating but declined to comment further.

It was not immediately clear what, if any, charges Ms. Blair faces.

Ms. Blair “experienced a medical emergency that led to the alleged conduct,” a representative for the actress said in a statement. “Upon landing, she received immediate medical attention and is currently in stable condition.”

The representative did not elaborate about the specifics of what led up to the episode or describe the nature of the medical emergency.

There were no operational issues on the flight. The plane landed ahead of schedule at J.F.K., according to FlightAware, a flight-tracking site.

Delta said in a statement that the airline “has zero tolerance for unruly or unlawful behavior, as the safety of our customers and crew always comes first.”

Ms. Blair was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in 2018, an autoimmune disease that attacks the central nervous system.

The actress, who has starred in the movies “Cruel Intentions” and “Hellboy,” has talked openly about the chronic illness, which was the subject of a documentary “Introducing, Selma Blair,” in 2021.

In 2016, Ms. Blair was removed from a flight from Cancun to Los Angeles after a disruptive outburst.

Ms. Blair said in a statement to Vanity Fair at the time that a combination of alcohol and medication caused her to “black out” and “say and do things that I deeply regret.”

item.title: Calls Show How Confusion Delayed Emergency Response for Christa Pike
item.description:
The emergency response to Christa Pike’s botched execution last month was delayed by about half an hour, because of confusion over the authenticity of the 911 call, according to dispatch and radio calls released on Monday.

The first 911 call for an ambulance was made by someone inside Riverbend Maximum Security Institution at 8:40 p.m. on Sept. 30, about an hour after the lethal injections there began, according to a redacted transcript of the phone call. But confirming the legitimacy of that call took several minutes of back and forth between Nashville emergency services and officials at the prison, according to audio from eight other calls and radio traffic, which was released as part of a public records request by several news organizations, including The New York Times.

The confusion seemed widespread. The initial 911 call did not come, as it might normally, from the central control at the Tennessee Department of Correction, and the caller did not have the right security verification.

In response, dispatch workers repeatedly tried to verify the call by reaching out to prison staff and other officials at the prison during the execution.

“We are trying to find out if that is an actual thing that is happening and we need to send an ambulance,” one caller said. Or, she added, “if this is someone that is just basically prank-calling.”

It appears from the phone calls that the Department of Correction’s central control was not immediately aware of the request for help.

One person at central control, who is not identified, tells Nashville emergency services that the department “would have been the one to call you guys — we didn’t call anyone.”

In another call, at 9:03 p.m., someone tells responders that supervisors have said “it is a false call” and that “there is no medical assistance needed.”

But at 9:07 p.m., an emergency responder says as part of radio traffic that “some sort of state official” is “outside the gate at the prison telling us that it’s real and demanding us to go in.”

Minutes later, they get word that prison officials have formally confirmed by phone that the request is legitimate.

The Tennessee Department of Correction did not immediately respond to a request for a comment about the apparent breakdown in communication. Previously, the agency said that every step of the protocol had been followed and the process did “not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out.”

Tennessee’s lethal injection protocol has come under renewed scrutiny after the failed attempt to carry out the execution of Ms. Pike, 50, who had been on death row for the torture and murder of Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old classmate in Knoxville. Lawyers for Ms. Pike, the first person to survive receiving two doses of the drug pentobarbital during an execution, said on Saturday that she had been discharged from a Nashville hospital and returned to prison.

The confusion captured on the calls appear to emphasize how the execution protocol, criticized by state defense lawyers and lawmakers in both parties for its vagueness, does not appear to account for problems during an execution. Tennessee has had two botched executions this year, including Ms. Pike’s.

The protocol really did not consider that the execution may not succeed, said Dr. Joel Zivot, an anesthesiologist and intensive care physician who consulted for Ms. Pike’s defense team before the failed execution.

Prison officials, he added, “had no idea that it could fail.”

Dr. Zivot was among the medical experts who warned that Ms. Pike’s underlying medical conditions, including small veins, could complicate the execution. Those warnings were ignored, her lawyers said.

“Considering, of course, what everyone said to them — that it could fail — they certainly did not seem to react,” Dr. Zivot said.

It was not clear from the recordings whether oxygen and other resuscitative gear were on hand in the execution chamber, or if Ms. Pike received medical care before an ambulance arrived more than an hour after the drugs were injected.

The transcript of the initial 911 call and some of the audio recordings were redacted, in part because Tennessee law prohibits the identification of anyone connected with execution procedures. But the person who made the initial 911 call appears unfamiliar with the steps needed to verify the legitimacy of an emergency call from the prison, leading to the effort to authenticate the call.

“Is nobody there that knows the process?” someone asks on a call between the Nashville Fire Department and emergency services.

“I have no idea,” someone else responds. “I guess because this is a special case, they may not know.”

The calls also show that Kelly Gleason, one of Ms. Pike’s lawyers, called 911 at 9:08 p.m., after a colleague who had witnessed the botched injections told her that Ms. Pike was still breathing.

“She is still alive and breathing and needs immediate lifesaving care,” Ms. Gleason said on her call for help. The ambulance drove through the gates a few minutes later.

item.title: 1 Rider Dies and Several Others Are Injured on a Georgia Roller Coaster
item.description:
One rider died and several others were injured on Monday on a roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia, the police said.

The Cobb County Police Department said in a statement that the episode happened at 3:58 p.m. at the amusement park in Austell, Ga., about 17 miles west of Atlanta.

Details about how the rider died, as well as the number of people injured and their conditions, were not immediately available.

A Six Flags representative said in a statement that park officials and the local authorities had responded immediately, but declined to describe what happened, citing the family’s privacy.

“We are deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today,” the representative said. “Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with the guest’s family, friends and loved ones.”

The representative also declined to say which roller coaster was involved.

Christina Morales contributed reporting.

This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

item.title: Trump, Playing Defense in Ohio, Tries to Shore Up Republicans in Tough Races
item.description:
President Trump returned to Ohio on Monday for the second time in 10 days to play defense in a state that twice helped deliver him to the White House.

He rallied in Youngstown, the heart of the industrial belt that helped fuel his rise, to marshal support for two of the Republican Party’s most vulnerable candidates this cycle: Senator Jon Husted, who is vying to retain his seat, and Vivek Ramaswamy, who is competing for the governorship.

They will need this area to break their way on Election Day in three weeks, with polls showing tight races in a state that Mr. Trump won in 2024 by 11 percentage points.

“Ohio is going to prove that America does not belong to those who hate it,” Mr. Trump said. “America belongs to those who love it.”

The Mahoning Valley, where he spoke, was battered by globalization. Many voters here grew up as Democrats but became Republicans after Mr. Trump persuaded them that he would fight for them when no one else had. Now, with prices persistently high and Mr. Trump’s approval rating hovering near a record low, officials with both parties see those voters as up for grabs.

“The Youngstown area for decades used to vote Democrat, and then you ran for office in 2016 and flipped it red forever,” Mr. Husted said on Monday in the arena, standing beside Mr. Trump. “Is that right, folks?”

The crowd whooped and cheered. There were at least two sections with large areas of empty seats.

On Monday, Mr. Trump announced two offerings to show voters in the region that he had their back: a new Defense Department facility, which he said would be based in Cleveland, to repair submarine components as well as a promise to make sure that a heat provider for Youngstown remained open.

In other battleground races, including in Michigan and Iowa, Republican candidates have tried to distance themselves from Mr. Trump. But in Ohio, the down-ballot candidates have stayed close to the president, relying on him to turn out the base in a year when Democratic enthusiasm appears to be high.

In addition to Mr. Husted and Mr. Ramaswamy, Representative Max Miller, the embattled congressional candidate accused of physically abusing his ex-wife and young daughter, was in the audience on Monday. (Mr. Miller has denied the allegations.) So was his estranged father-in-law, Senator Bernie Moreno, the Republican who beat Mr. Husted’s Democratic opponent, former Senator Sherrod Brown, two years ago.

Mr. Trump returned the favor by lavishing praise on the candidates — most of all on Mr. Husted, a former football player, who appeared to have impressed the president with his physicality.

“I don’t do this with men very often,” Mr. Trump said. “I started examining his body, because I didn’t know he was a great athlete.”

item.title: Trump Says He Is ‘Looking at’ Firing Kimberly Guilfoyle
item.description:
President Trump said on Monday that he was “looking at” firing Kimberly Guilfoyle, the U.S. ambassador to Greece, following revelations that she had asked a Republican donor to pay her credit card bill in exchange for access to senior Trump administration officials.

“Well, we’re looking at it, yeah,” Mr. Trump said when asked by a reporter whether he was thinking of firing Ms. Guilfoyle. “We’re not happy.”

The donor, Eric Deters, said last week that Ms. Guilfoyle had asked him to wire $100,000 to pay off her American Express card just before her Senate confirmation hearing in July 2025. She promised to serve as his “ride or die in Trump world” if he did, according to what appeared to be screenshots of their correspondence that Mr. Deters provided to The New York Times.

“Honey please I need you to get this done for me today,” she wrote in what appeared to be a text message.

Ms. Guilfoyle, who was once engaged to Mr. Trump’s oldest son, Donald Trump Jr., was one of the first ambassadors to be nominated in the president’s second term.

The texts suggest that Ms. Guilfoyle warned Mr. Deters to call her on Signal and to keep their interactions private. “You’ll literally cost me my ambassadorship,” she wrote, according to one of the screenshots.

Neither the State Department nor the U.S. Embassy in Athens responded immediately to requests for comment late Monday. A lawyer for Ms. Guilfoyle previously declined to comment on the correspondence.

The accusations against Ms. Guilfoyle are the latest allegations of misconduct to emerge against her. Greeks interviewed on Athens in recent days have expressed exasperation and cynicism over reports of her dealings.

item.title: The New Affordability Fight in the Midterms: Home Insurance Prices
item.description:
In Florida, as Hurricane Isaias blasted through the panhandle, the candidates for governor jousted over who could best tame the highest home insurance rates in the country.

In North Carolina, where flooding and skyrocketing construction costs have lifted premiums, voters are weighing a constitutional amendment to cap property taxes.

And in Kansas, where hail storms and intense winds have pushed the cost of insuring a house into the top five nationwide, a usually sleepy race for insurance commissioner is surprisingly fierce.

In the angry debate over soaring costs of living this campaign season, the price of keeping a roof overhead — specifically insurance and property taxes — has joined gas, diesel, and groceries as a top voter concern three weeks before the midterm elections.

Rising homeowners rates — driven by the fires, hurricanes and tornadoes worsened by climate change — have helped put reliably Republican states like Kansas and Florida onto the battlefield, pushed North Carolina toward the Democrats and roiled Democratic politics in California.

Home-insurance premiums have climbed 46 percent since 2021, nearly triple the rate of inflation. One recent survey found that 58 percent of Americans said rising insurance costs would make them more likely to vote.

In another poll conducted in Arizona, Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska and North Carolina, respondents overwhelmingly wanted elected officials to do more to reduce premiums and hold companies more accountable.

Nearly one-third of North Carolinians and more than a quarter of Kansans said they had postponed major purchases or life decisions because of insurance spikes.

That has forced politicians to respond.

“We’re going to go to bat for them,” Daniel Hawkins, the Republican Speaker of the Kansas House running for insurance commissioner, promised voters at a recent fund-raiser in Wichita. And if insurance companies make people’s lives difficult, he warned, “I will be their worst nightmare.”

Hurricanes and wildfires might grab the headlines, but out of the 10 most expensive states for home insurance, six sit in the nation’s midsection, in high-risk corridors known as Tornado Alley and Hail Alley.

In Kansas, where insurance claim payouts have nearly doubled in two years to $879 million, the annual premium for a $300,000 house with a $1,000 deductible is now $5,289 — 84 percent higher than the national average.

Two years ago, Sarah Lopez-Lewis and her husband, Brent Lewis, Wichita natives with backgrounds in health care and education, were informed by their mortgage company that their monthly payment would jump from $3,000 to $4,000, driven by taxes and insurance.

The timing was brutal. With their twin toddler daughters requiring specialized medical care, the Lewises had left their jobs to launch a nonprofit focused on affordable child care. Reluctantly, they put their house on the market and moved last month into a townhouse rental in a Kansas City exurb closer to the girls’ doctors.

“It’s harder and harder to take care of all the things we need and the taxes to pay — the weather’s changing and insurance is harder and harder to afford,” Mr. Lewis said.

One thing within their control, though, is voting for a new insurance commissioner to regulate the rates and conduct of home, health and auto insurance companies.

Mr. Hawkins’ opponent, State Senator Dinah Sykes, the chamber’s Democratic leader, represents Johnson County, outside Kansas City, Kan. Elected in 2016 as a Republican, she was one of four legislators, all women, to switch parties two years later, uncomfortable with the party’s rightward tilt.

A self-described “data nerd,” Ms. Sykes, 49, wants the office to do more to protect consumers. She says that her lack of ties to the insurance industry gives her a fresh perspective, in contrast to Mr. Hawkins, an employee benefits consultant with decades of experience in insurance.

“I don’t think you should have the fox guarding the henhouse,” she said at a fund-raiser at the home of David Toland, the state’s term-limited lieutenant governor and commerce secretary, in Iola, Kan.

Mr. Hawkins, 65, acknowledged that national headwinds may affect state Republicans, but he said his conservative legislative record and business background would help him “hit the ground running,” if elected.

“Do you want somebody that has 32 years of experience and extensive knowledge of the insurance industry, or do you want somebody to come in and fake it until they make it?” asked Mr. Hawkins, who was first elected as a state representative in 2012.

Two other states are electing new insurance commissioners in November — California and Oklahoma — while Georgia’s Republican incumbent is seeking re-election.

California voters will choose between two Democrats: State Senator Ben Allen, who represents the Pacific Palisades area destroyed by last year’s wildfires, and Jane Kim, a former San Francisco supervisor, who has rolled out a single-payer, state-run disaster plan modeled after New Zealand.

In Oklahoma, Bob Sullivan, an insurance executive who ran a populist campaign to “Make Insurance Fair Again,” upset the Republican establishment’s preferred candidate, a longtime legislator, in the primary. Oklahoma voters are also weighing a constitutional amendment to lower annual property assessment caps.

In Florida, Representative Byron Donalds, the Republican nominee for governor, and former Representative David Jolly, his Democratic opponent, have clashed over home insurance and a ballot measure expanding homestead property tax exemptions.

Supporters of the measure argue it will aid homeowners crushed by surging insurance costs, while critics warn that local governments would be starved of funds for schools and emergency services.

“When people have affordability challenges, I think there can be this sort of knee-jerk response by saying we should just suppress prices everywhere to help people,” said Carolyn Kousky, an economist and founder of Insurance for Good, a nonprofit focused on climate risk and disaster recovery.

The burden of insurance has gotten to the point where an estimated one-in-seven homeowners are opting to go without insurance to pay other bills.

In Wyandotte County and Kansas City, Kan., that group includes Gilbert Kirk, 71. He was watching late-night television with his dog Beetle in mid-August when a severe storm tore through his house, trapping him under debris for hours, until a neighbor pulled him out.

Weeks later, the house remains uninhabitable. On his to-do list if he moves back? Getting insurance.

“I had everything I needed and then the next minute, man, it’s all gone,” he said. “You just feel empty.”

item.title: He Would Be Florida’s First Black Governor. Can He Sway Black Voters?
item.description:
The Black men at the Caribbean restaurant outside Miami wanted to hear how Byron Donalds would fix Florida’s soaring cost of living when he stopped there to mingle this month.

But they also pressed him about whether he would be a puppet for another Florida voter: Donald J. Trump, the increasingly unpopular president.

Mr. Donalds, the Republican congressman hoping to become Florida’s first Black governor, assured them during the private meal in Miami Gardens, Fla., that he was on the ballot — not Mr. Trump.

“I was persuaded,” said Drumene Woodside, 53, who said he would cast his ballot for Mr. Donalds though he normally votes for Democrats.

Mr. Donalds is working to win over Black Floridians like Mr. Woodside in the stretch run, as his party girds for the possibility of low turnout among many of the voters who powered Mr. Trump to victory two years ago.

The race has been surprisingly competitive for a state that has been reliably red for well over a decade. Mr. Donalds’s Democratic opponent is David Jolly, a white former Republican congressman who left the party in 2018.

In recent weeks, Mr. Donalds has held several campaign events focused on Black voters, including a forum at Florida A&M University, the historically Black college he attended in the 1990s, where he was grilled by some of the students in attendance.

He is rolling out endorsements from local Black leaders, including longtime Democrats. He is also buying ads in news outlets with large Black audiences in voter-rich South Florida, and visiting Black churches to share his conservative vision. His campaign staff includes Janiyah Thomas, who was the Black media director for the Trump campaign in 2024.

It’s an uphill battle in a state where Black voters have historically backed Democrats by wide margins. Florida, with more than 13 million registered voters, has fewer than 100,000 Black Republicans.

On a recent Saturday, at a lightly attended event in Overtown, a historically Black neighborhood of Miami, some attendees were affiliated with a faith-based nonprofit and said they had been driven in from two counties away.

Another attendee, Kalyn James of Miami, wore a pin endorsing Angie Nixon, a Black Democratic state legislator running for the U.S. Senate. Ms James watched quietly holding a small “Vote Blue” sign as the candidate spoke.

She said she attended to hear Mr. Donalds’s pitch, but was unconvinced that his support for Republican policies would be good for Black people.

Voters have elected only three Black governors in the country’s history, all Democrats, and none further south than Virginia.

But this year, the two major parties are fielding seven Black gubernatorial candidates. Three are Republicans: Mr. Donalds; Representative John James of Michigan; and Lisa Demuth, the speaker of the Minnesota House of Representatives.

In Florida, Democrats have not held the governor’s mansion since the 1990s. Andrew Gillum, a Black Democrat who was the mayor of Tallahassee, narrowly lost in 2018 to Ron DeSantis, a white Republican who has since cemented Florida into a conservative bastion.

Mr. Trump made inroads with Black and Hispanic voters nationally in 2024. But as he faces sagging approval ratings, that fragile coalition is fraying and many Republican candidates are downplaying their ties to the president.

Overall, Mr. Donalds remains favored in the governor’s race. There are 1.5 million more registered Republicans than Democrats in the state, and he won Mr. Trump’s endorsement before he even declared his candidacy.

But in the primary, Mr. Donalds underperformed with white voters in rural counties. If that pattern holds in a tight general election, support from Black voters will be crucial, said Sean Freeder, an associate professor of political science at the University of North Florida and the director of its Public Opinion Research Lab.

A native of New York City who moved to Florida for college, Mr. Donalds was raised by a single mother who voted Democrat. His family has roots in Panama and Jamaica. On the campaign trail, he has mostly downplayed the significance of potentially becoming the first elected Black governor in the South.

Instead, Mr. Donalds has described Florida as a “great meritocracy,” pitching plans to address the affordability crisis, lower insurance costs and build businesses.

At the Florida A&M event, he urged Black students to stop moving “as a monolith” for Democrats.

“You’ve been faithful to that party,” Mr. Donalds said. “Have they been faithful to you?”

Black voters often perceive him as doing Mr. Trump’s bidding, Mr. Donalds told reporters this month at Lorna’s Caribbean & American Grill, the restaurant in Miami Gardens where he made a campaign stop.

“That’s not true. I have my own thoughts, my own opinions, I have my own ideas,” he said after meeting with a small group of Black voters over conch fritters, oxtail with peas and jerk chicken.

Jude Civil, 56, who had volunteered for past Democratic gubernatorial campaigns, was not wholly sold. But he appreciated Mr. Donalds’s willingness to field tough questions.

“He’s a lot closer than he was before,” Mr. Civil said of Mr. Donalds’s chances of landing his vote.

Three men at the event said they also planned to vote for Ms. Nixon, who has energized Black voters across Florida. Donalds supporters are hoping that at least some Black voters who turn out for Ms. Nixon will split their ticket and vote for him, too.

Black leaders around the state are divided over Mr. Donalds’s candidacy, with many expressing unease about his support for Mr. Trump and Mr. DeSantis. Many have bristled at Mr. DeSantis’s efforts to curb diversity initiatives, rewrite state history lessons on race and reshape Congressional districts, decreasing Black elected representation.

“I will forfeit having the first Black governor any day, especially when it’s someone who has participated in the degradation of our people,” said State Senator Shevrin D. Jones, a Democrat who represents part of Miami-Dade County and advises the Jolly campaign.

Still, Mr. Donalds has won the support of some Black Democrats who were upset that Mr. Jolly did not choose a Black running mate, and instead picked Gwen Graham, whose father was former Gov. Bob Graham.

“We have people who are overqualified for the position to serve as lieutenant governor, and yet all those people were passed over,” said Cynthia Chestnut, a Black Democratic city commissioner in Gainesville who endorsed Mr. Donalds.

Mr. Jolly, who has described Mr. Donalds as having an “anti-Black agenda,” is also aggressively courting Black voters. On Sunday, he appeared with the Rev. Al Sharpton and Ben Crump, the civil rights lawyer, at Bethel Missionary Baptist Church in Tallahassee.

At another Black church recently, Antioch Missionary Baptist in Miami Gardens, Mr. Jolly energized the crowd by quoting Bible scripture and imploring people to turn to God.

He impressed Joseph Grant III, a parishioner who said he had been disturbed by a comment Mr. Donalds had made in 2024, while campaigning for Mr. Trump, that “more Black people voted conservatively” during the Jim Crow era of racial segregation.

Black Democrats criticized the comment at the time; Mr. Donalds has repeatedly said it was taken out of context.

Others in the congregation said they were bothered by Mr. Donalds’s unwavering support for the president.

“I hear a lot of Trump in him, and his ideology is not sitting right with me,” said the Rev. Rodney Pinder, 72.

Back in Miami, at the Overtown event, Amanda Bazil, 30, pressed Mr. Donalds on the quality of private schools that have exploded in numbers since the state extended tuition aid in 2023. Ms. Bazil, who is Haitian American, said she was somewhat reassured by his answer — but that he had not yet won her vote.

One of her concerns: Mr. Donalds’s support for Mr. Trump’s aggressive immigration enforcement, including ending legal protections that allowed 330,000 Haitians to live and work in the United States. Some of her relatives are worried about being deported.

“It’s very disheartening,” Ms. Bazil said.

Valerie Crowder contributed reporting from Tallahassee, Fla.

]]>

item.title: These California Boat Dwellers Fear the Worst: Life on Land
item.description:
Chad Wycliffe lives on a bay with a front-row view of the San Francisco skyline. Waves lull him to sleep. He’s surrounded by hills dotted with multimillion-dollar mansions and marinas with luxury yachts.

He doesn’t pay any rent.

His home is a half-century-old sailboat with a faded red jib and barnacles growing beneath it. At 45, Mr. Wycliffe, has lived on the water for nearly half of his life.

He first moved to Richardson Bay, just north of the city, as a troubled teen drawn to the thrill of the open water. There, a group of mariners, exiles and artists who called themselves “anchor outs” lived aboard vessels less than a mile — but worlds away — from ordinary society.

To many, the bay was a refuge. To officials and some Marin residents, however, the collection of boats was more like a floating homeless encampment.

Now, the community, one of the last vestiges of counterculture in the Bay Area, has been all but dismantled. Officials say Richardson Bay will be cleared of the last “illegally anchored vessels” by Thursday.

Mr. Wycliffe is one of the final holdouts.

“They’re having a hard time finding out how to get me out of here,” he said. “They’re going to have to kill me.”

Richardson Bay is a shallow arm of the San Francisco Bay in Marin County, one of the most expensive places to live in the country. It’s surrounded by waterfront cities, including Sausalito, a former shipbuilding town that now has a promenade of galleries, white-tablecloth restaurants and gift stores selling trinkets and T-shirts with the slogan “Keep Sausalito Salty.”

For decades, the sailboats floating on the bay were part of the scene. “It was a painting,” said Jeff Scharosch, a general manager and partner at The Spinnaker, a glass-walled restaurant suspended over the water. But he and some other locals also considered the boats a blight and a hazard.

“I used to to tell people, ‘Yeah, they look beautiful from afar because you don’t see that they’re barely seaworthy,” he said.

Officials said many of the boats were unsafe or abandoned, and that their anchors and chains were damaging the bay’s eelgrass beds, a marine habitat that sequesters carbon. About a decade ago, the authorities began a concerted effort to remove and destroy boats they said were abandoned or derelict.

In Sausalito, many residents are opposing a measure that would allow large-scale development that they fear will push out boatyards and maritime trades, turning their waterfront into one that more closely resembles Miami Beach.

Sophia Collier, a Sausalito-based investor and sculptor said she saw the campaign to remove the anchor outs as part of that broader effort to gentrify the region and force out nonconformists.

“The anchor outs are the edge,” she said. “Those are our saltiest residents.”

Richardson Bay historically has drawn the free-spirited, the outcast and the priced out. After its World War II shipyard closed in the late 1940s, veterans and artists moved into the abandoned vessels and barges.

By the 1970s, hundreds of people lived in a sprawling waterfront neighborhood of makeshift houseboats and homes built from salvaged materials. They had their own newspaper, and an offshore settlement, known as Dredgetown. . Many got by on a mix of odd jobs, bartering and scavenging.

Over the years, efforts to clear the waterfront sparked violent clashes, known as the Houseboat Wars, with the authorities. Most of the houseboats were ultimately regulated and brought into onshore marinas.

Some anchor outs, however, remained or moved into the open bay. As economic conditions grew worse in the Bay Area, the flotilla mushroomed, expanding to nearly 250 boats by 2016, according to official counts. Mr. Wycliffe and other anchor outs said that the water provided solace to those who didn’t conform to life on land.

“The water was just like a magnetic source for me,” he said. “And the people that were here, they were real.”

At the same time, some locals became fed up with the boats. Some complained of refuse and human waste dumped into the bay. Others cited safety concerns: during storms, boats often broke loose and crashed ashore. Others caught fire, collided, or sunk.

“It was kind of the Wild, Wild West,” Mr. Scharosch said. He recalled that on a couple of occasions, boats came close to hitting the restaurant.

Richard Ashlock, one of the last anchor outs, said he felt the true mariners deserved to stay on the water. But he acknowledged that others had moved there with little experience or respect.

“When all the rents went up in Oakland, Berkeley, and San Francisco, a lot of people ended up losing their apartments, but you could get boats for a song,” he said. “They were just desperate to have a place to live, and I never blamed them for that. What I did blame them for was their boats were completely trashed.”

Mr. Ashlock, 75, recalled paddling his kayak up to the side of boats that had dumped trash into the water, then throwing it back to them with a warning that the anchorage would be shuttered. He and others dispute the eelgrass concerns, arguing that their vessels are like floating ecosystems and that onshore activities are far more polluting.

Officials approved a plan last week for Mr. Ashlock to move his boat to a marina, where he will earn his keep as a caretaker, although he remained on the bay as of early October.

In 2022, officials began offering the anchor outs $150 per foot for their surrendered boats and, the following year, offered temporary housing vouchers under a $3 million state grant. As of this month, the Richardson Bay Regional Agency, which has been responsible for clearing the bay, had removed more than 500 boats from the water. Temporary housing was provided to 52 former anchor outs, said Brad Gross, the agency’s executive director.

The program was designed to place the anchor outs in apartments for a year, with the goal of transitioning them to permanent federal housing. But that pipeline broke down in May 2025, after rising rental costs exhausted the housing authority's budget. Permanent federal housing vouchers remain limited, Mr. Gross said.

Some forced from the anchorage have ended up displaced.

Meredith Rodas, 56, who lived on the anchorage for two decades, said that she and her husband had applied for housing vouchers, but didn’t receive them. Last month, they were living with their two dogs in a pickup truck at a marina about 10 miles from Sausalito.

“It’s a disaster,” she said.

Mr. Gross said that those who fell through the cracks had been referred to housing officials. “We’re not a housing program,” he said. “Our housing program was very, very specific with a very specific target audience, and we were able to accommodate those that were interested.”

Some who were lucky enough to get housing have welcomed the comforts of moving ashore. In his final days on the anchorage, Peter Glaser, 65, said he couldn’t believe he would have a bathtub, washer and dryer, and walk-in closet.

Still, he was miserable at the prospect.

“I’m depressed that they basically won,” Mr. Glaser said from below deck on the sailboat he shared with his cat, piled with books and mementos. “They’ve managed to obliterate our community that’s been around for 70 years,” he said.

Mr. Wycliffe insists that he will remain on the water. When officials ordered him to leave, he applied for housing, he said, but was not offered anything he felt could accommodate himself and his two dogs.

So Mr. Wycliffe moved farther offshore, beyond the reach of the local officials.

Out on the open water, large swells make getting between his skiff and his sailboat treacherous. A fall overboard could leave him alone in the dark, freezing cold. But he can see no viable alternative.

Mr. Wycliffe is afraid of who he might become on land.

“I’ve lived this way for so long that I don’t really know how to live any other way,” he said. “It’s weird saying that because people would think that, well, it’s more dangerous to live out here.”

“Maybe,” he observed. “But I’d rather die out here.”

Alain Delaquérière contributed research.
